items.label: Turning Points 02
items.summary: BBC Radio Cambridgeshire, 2019, live. The quiet son who never spoke up, on air across the county. So what changed?
items.petal:
The quiet son who never spoke up, live on BBC Radio Cambridgeshire.

2019. “On air in 3… 2… 1…” And the voice going out across the county was mine. I grew up deferring to a strong father. I was the one who listened, never the one who spoke.

No big leap changed that. A staircase of small, frightening steps did, and I never climbed it alone.

I didn't find courage, then act. I acted, and courage followed.

What's something you did scared that you're now glad you did?

items.label: Turning Points 03
items.summary: Every test came back normal. Every doctor said I was fine. Every part of me said I wasn't.
items.petal:
Every test came back normal. Every part of me said I wasn't fine.

2000. Newly qualified, and a virus I couldn't name had begun to affect my heart. The advice was kind and simple: “Just keep taking ibuprofen.” I took the tablets. Feeling fine never came.

So I stopped waiting. I became a locum, searched inward, and found meditation in India. It didn't replace medicine. It gave me steadiness while I healed.

Sometimes the quietest voice in the room is the one telling the truth.

When did you last trust a feeling nobody else could see?

items.label: Turning Points 04
items.summary: New Zealand, 2005. My cousin's wedding, and I'd been asked to be the MC. That's how I met Liril.
items.petal:
The quiet boy who never left home was handed a microphone.

New Zealand, 2005. My cousin's wedding, and I'd been asked to be the MC. A few years earlier, I'd have found a polite reason to say no.

This time, I picked it up. That's how I met Liril. She saw straight into my blind spot, and believed in the man I could become.

Step up when you're asked. You never know who's in the room.

Who saw something in you before you could see it yourself?

items.label: Turning Points 05
items.summary: Not for university. Not for my first job. Not once. Comfort doesn't feel like a cage. It feels like love.
items.petal:
Not for university. Not for my first job. Not once.

My parents had crossed continents to give us a future. They cooked, they organised, they decided, and I let them. I studied optometry and travelled home every evening, quietly believing I couldn't survive on my own.

It would take an illness, a journey to India and a stranger's spare key before I finally stepped outside that door.

A bird that is always fed never learns to fly.

What comfort in your life might quietly be holding you back?

items.label: Science and Spirit 02
items.summary: 6/6 is the line on the chart we all aim for. For a long time, I thought it meant a job well done. It doesn't.
items.petal:
6/6 is the line on the chart we all aim for. It isn't the finish line.

For years, I thought reaching it meant a job well done. But you can reach 6/6 and still send someone home unhappy: uncomfortable, confused, rushed.

In my specialist contact lens work, I learned that success is the moment someone blinks, looks up and says, “That's it. That feels right.”

Vision belongs to the eye. Perception belongs to the heart.

When did someone last make you feel truly seen?

items.label: Turning Points 06
items.summary: 2001. A borrowed house in St Neots, and my first time living away from my parents. It was frightening.
items.petal:
The first night in someone else's house, I didn't know where anything was.

2001. A woman I'd met on a mountain in India asked me to look after her home in St Neots. I was living away from my parents for the first time.

I learned to shop, budget and sit with my own company. In the evenings I meditated, and strangers became friends. Independence felt like meeting myself.

The life we're meant to live is often waiting just outside the door we fear most.

What did you learn about yourself the first time you stood on your own?

items.label: Turning Points 07
items.summary: Ten till five. Free parking. Fifteen minutes from home. I could have stayed there for the rest of my career.
items.petal:
Ten till five. Free parking. Fifteen minutes from home.

As a locum, I'd found a supermarket practice that ticked every box. Easy. Predictable. I could have stayed there for the rest of my career, and nobody would have blamed me.

Then I got married. My wife looked at my comfortable routine and asked: is this really all you want? So I began, slowly, to stretch.

Like the muscles of the eye, we need challenge to stay strong.

Who in your life refuses to let you settle?

items.label: Science and Spirit 03
items.summary: Every time you blink, a film thinner than a hair keeps your eye seeing. Tears are not a weakness.
items.petal:
Every time you blink, a film thinner than a hair keeps your eye seeing.

I spend much of my working life treating dry eye, and I've seen how much suffering a missing tear can cause. Tears are not a weakness of the eye.

Yet so many of us were taught to hold our own tears back. In my darkest moments, it was often after I finally let them come that I could see the way forward again.

Clarity often arrives on the other side of feeling.

When did letting yourself feel something help you see more clearly?

items.label: Turning Points 08
items.summary: It began with a moment of kindness. And a mistake.
items.petal:
It began with a moment of kindness. And a mistake.

A stressed teenager sat in my consulting chair, his mother elsewhere in the store. I told him about Sahaja Yoga meditation. My heart was in the right place. My judgement was not. A complaint followed, and nearly two years of waiting.

I took one day a week at Clamp and began teaching. Then the letter came: no action taken. Within a year, I was a director.

What felt like punishment was redirection.

Which of your “mistakes” might one day turn out to be your turning point?

items.label: Turning Points 09
items.summary: 2017 was one of the hardest years I have known. So I took the small opportunities in front of me.
items.petal:
Two single days a week. That's all it was.

2017 was one of the hardest years I have known. I didn't feel brave, just unsettled. So I took the small opportunities in front of me: a day at Clamp in Cambridge, more teaching at Anglia Ruskin.

Then the practice's director moved on. Because I was already there, already trusted, I was offered the role. By 2018, I was Clinical Director, alongside my partner David.

The hardest year of my life was quietly preparing the best ones.

What small step are you underestimating right now?

items.label: Turning Points 10
items.summary: There's one name missing from every trophy we've ever lifted. Everyone's.

items.label: Science and Spirit 04
items.summary: Pass white light through a prism and it opens into a rainbow. The colours were there all along.
items.petal:
Pass white light through a prism and it opens into a rainbow.

As light slows, it bends, and each colour bends a slightly different amount. The colours were there all along. It took the bending to reveal them.

The moments that bent me, the illness, the uncertainty, the hard years, slowed me down. And in slowing down, I found patience, compassion, stillness and gratitude.

I wouldn't have chosen those passages. But I wouldn't give back what they revealed.

What has a difficult season revealed in you?

items.label: Turning Points 11
items.summary: In 2020, at 42, I began training as an Independent Prescriber. Twenty years after qualifying, I sat exams again.

items.label: Turning Points 12
items.summary: I walked in expecting to share what I knew. Week after week, I walked out having learned more than I taught.

items.label: Turning Points 13
items.summary: Some days, work is the calmest place in my life.
items.petal:
Some days, work is the calmest place in my life.

At the practice, a patient brings a problem and we solve it. At home, people I love are facing illnesses I can't cure. There's no prescription for watching someone you love struggle.

I can't control what happens to them. But I can control how present I am. Whether I listen. Whether I turn up, even when there's nothing to fix.

Love doesn't ask us to fix everything. Just to be there.

What are you trying to control that is asking only for your presence?

items.label: The Inner Journey 01
items.summary: What if spiritual growth isn't about becoming someone new, but rediscovering who we were before the world shaped us?
items.petal:
What if spiritual growth is rediscovering who we were before the world shaped us?

As small boys, my sons laughed without calculating and loved without keeping score. Then we grow up and learn to compete and compare. By my twenties, I'd almost forgotten how to simply be.

In Sahaja Yoga, the Mooladhara is the centre of innocence: covered over, never truly lost. In meditation, something simpler began to return.

Growing spiritually may mean becoming less complicated, not more impressive.

What has life hardened in you that is now ready to soften?

items.label: Turning Points 14
items.summary: When people meet me, they see the suit, the smile, the practice.
items.petal:
When people meet me, they see the suit, the smile, the practice.

They don't always know I grew up with vitiligo. As a boy, I knew what it felt like to be looked at, not seen. Long sleeves. Careful angles. Quiet corners.

Then I realised the people who mattered most weren't looking at my skin. They were looking at me. That's where my whole philosophy of care began.

Being looked at makes us smaller. Being seen gives us back our size.

When did someone first make you feel seen, rather than looked at?

items.label: The Inner Journey 02
items.summary: We have become experts at thinking. But have we forgotten how to be still?
items.petal:
We have become experts at thinking. But have we forgotten how to be still?

I know the pattern well. Driving home from Cambridge, replaying a conversation. Sitting at dinner, mentally answering tomorrow's emails.

On the mountain in India where I first learned to meditate, I experienced a few seconds without a single thought. Not emptiness. Peace. Like an eye that stares too long, the mind needs to look away before clarity returns.

The mind is a wonderful instrument and a poor master.

Are your thoughts helping you live, or have they become the place you live?

items.label: Turning Points 15
items.summary: When my sons were small, they followed me everywhere.
items.petal:
When my sons were small, they followed me everywhere.

To the shops. To gatherings. To meditation. Now they're teenagers, choosing their own paths, and some of what matters deeply to me doesn't matter to them right now. That was harder to accept than I expected.

But it isn't rejection. It's growth. I want them to choose freely, not follow me out of duty.

Parenting isn't steering. It's bending a little light their way, and trusting them with the rest.

Who are you learning to love by letting go?

items.label: The Inner Journey 03
items.summary: There's always another achievement waiting to make us happy. So why does satisfaction stay just out of reach?
items.petal:
There's always another achievement waiting to make us happy.

Becoming a director. Awards for our practice. A distinction as an Independent Prescriber. Each brought real joy, and each time another target quietly appeared.

In Sahaja Yoga, the Nabhi is associated with contentment and balance. Meditation gives me a moment to notice desire, rather than automatically obey it.

Contentment isn't complacency. It's seeing what we already have.

If nothing in your life changed tomorrow, what could you still be grateful for today?

items.label: Turning Points 16
items.summary: My parents live across the road from us now.
items.petal:
My parents live across the road from us now.

I didn't leave home until my twenties. My parents did everything for me. Two years ago, I encouraged them to move up to St Neots so I could help.

Now I'm the one popping over with shopping, sorting appointments, checking all is well. It isn't always easy. But there are cups of tea, old stories, and my sons with their grandparents.

The boy who couldn't leave home has become the son who brought them home.

Who once carried you, whom you now have the chance to carry?

items.label: The Inner Journey 04
items.summary: It's possible to know a great deal about life and still struggle to guide your own.
items.petal:
It's possible to know a great deal about life and still struggle to guide your own.

I grew up looking to others to tell me what was right. In my pottery classes, I'm learning how hard it is to centre clay on the wheel. Push too hard and it collapses.

In Sahaja Yoga, the Void represents the inner guru: our own discernment. Mastery is a quiet, steady pressure from the centre.

Becoming our own master means taking responsibility for ourselves.

Where are you waiting for someone else to develop the wisdom you could grow within yourself?

items.label: Turning Points 17
items.summary: My father met his own father properly only as a young man. Within a year, he had died.
items.petal:
Two brothers, raised on different continents, suddenly sharing one small house.

My grandfather went to Africa to work, taking his eldest son. My father grew up without a father, protecting his mother. Years later, the family reunited in England, all under one roof.

It should have been a disaster. Instead, slowly, they became friends. Then close. Then family in the truest sense.

Relationships are built one meal, one argument, one forgiveness at a time.

Which relationship in your life is worth building again, from the beginning?

items.label: The Inner Journey 05
items.summary: Our closest relationships often teach us our greatest lessons about love.
items.petal:
Our closest relationships often teach us our greatest lessons about love.

My wife believed in me before I believed in myself. Our two teenage sons are the greatest privilege of my life, and the most humbling. And family life exposes our expectations.

So I keep asking: do the people closest to me experience my love in the way I intend it?

Love is revealed by how freely we let others be themselves.

Are you loving the people in your life as they are, or as you'd like them to become?

items.label: Turning Points 18
items.summary: My grandmother was married at twelve or thirteen.
items.petal:
My grandmother was married at twelve or thirteen.

She never learned to read or write. Her brothers went to school. She did not. She lost her mother young, raised her children largely alone, and still held the family together.

Three generations later, I went to university, qualified, and at 42 went back to study again. Every week, I teach students.

Every letter she never learned to write is part of why I'll never stop learning.

Whose sacrifice made your opportunities possible?

items.label: The Inner Journey 06
items.summary: We remember the words that hurt us. How often do we remember the words we've used to hurt others?
items.petal:
We remember the words that hurt us. Do we remember the ones we've used to hurt others?

In the consulting room, how we speak matters as much as what we say. Yet so often, the people we love most get the least careful version of us.

Before speaking, I try to ask: Is it true? Is it helpful? Can I say it without wounding someone's dignity?

Our words last only a moment. Their echoes can last a lifetime.

Would the people closest to you recognise your love in the way you spoke to them this week?

items.label: Turning Points 19
items.summary: From the outside, my early twenties looked fine. I'd qualified as an optometrist. I had a profession, a family, a future.
items.petal:
From the outside, my early twenties looked fine.

A profession, a family, a future. Inside, I was going through the motions, deferring to everyone and quietly not at peace. Men of my background often didn't talk about it.

Then an illness nobody could explain stopped me in my tracks. I wasn't living my life. I was living a life.

Admitting you're not fine isn't weakness. It's the beginning of honesty.

If you stopped going through the motions, what would you want your life to feel like?

items.label: The Inner Journey 07
items.summary: How much of our present are we giving away to something that happened in the past?
items.petal:
How much of our present are we giving away to something that happened in the past?

Most of us carry an archive of old hurts. I've carried my share, replaying certain moments far more often than they deserved.

In Sahaja Yoga, the Agnya is the centre of forgiveness. Its simplest affirmation is two words: “I forgive.” Sometimes that begins as a decision, long before it becomes a feeling.

Forgiveness doesn't rewrite the past. It changes the hold the past has on us.

What are you still carrying that no longer helps you become who you want to be?

items.label: Science and Spirit 05
items.summary: Walk from a bright room into darkness, and at first you see nothing. Then, slowly, shapes appear. The edge of a door. A chair. A window.
items.petal:
Walk from a bright room into darkness, and at first you see nothing.

Then, slowly, shapes appear. The eye's rods can take twenty minutes or more to adjust. The darkness hasn't changed. Your eyes have.

Some seasons feel like that dark room. The temptation is to grab for the light switch. But if we stay a little longer, without fighting it, a path appears.

We see more in the dark than we expect, if we give ourselves time.

What might you see if you gave your eyes a little longer to adjust?

items.label: The Inner Journey 08
items.summary: What if peace begins when we stop demanding an answer to every question?
items.petal:
What if peace begins when we stop demanding an answer to every question?

My profession is built on understanding. But soon after qualifying, I became unwell and every test came back normal. All that science, and no answer.

On a mountain in India, I experienced something I couldn't explain and didn't need to: a cool stillness. Meditation never replaced medicine for me. It gave me steadiness alongside it.

The mind can describe peace. Meditation invites us to experience it.

Could you sit quietly for a few minutes without needing to solve, judge or explain anything?

items.label: Science and Spirit 06
items.summary: Hold your gaze on a single word on this page.
items.petal:
Hold your gaze on a single word on this page.

Without moving your eyes, notice what's around it. That's peripheral vision: not sharp, but remarkably good at noticing movement.

Most of us live in our central vision, and miss the colleague who's gone quiet, the parent slowing down, the child who needs a moment. In the practice, I train myself to notice the edges. At home, I'm still learning.

The most important things often arrive at the edges.

Who is at the edge of your vision right now, waiting to be noticed?

items.label: The Inner Journey 09
items.summary: Can we truly grow spiritually if it makes us less compassionate towards others?
items.petal:
Can we truly grow spiritually if it makes us less compassionate towards others?

In St Neots, I found others drawn to the same stillness, and we began meditating together. That small circle carried me through uncertain years. At work, every award belongs to a team.

In Sahaja Yoga, collectivity is central to growth: not losing ourselves, but recognising our shared humanity.

The real question isn't how spiritual I feel. It's whether I'm easier to live and work with.

Does your inner growth make you kinder to be around, or simply more certain you're right?

items.label: The Inner Journey 10
items.summary: Spiritual growth isn't a straight line. It's a living process.
items.petal:
Spiritual growth isn't a straight line.

The boy who never left home. An illness no one could explain. A mountain in India and a stranger's spare key. Two small days a week that became a directorship. Times of peace, and times I fell straight back into old habits.

The danger isn't that we fall. It's that we stop noticing.

Rise. Fall. Watch. Correct. Grow. That is the living ascent.

What one small change today would bring your actions closer to the person you want to become?
